Baselines are not fully convincing. Scene-specific distractor-free methods are adapted into the MVSplat training loss in ad hoc ways, sometimes omitting important components, so the comparisons may understate what stronger or properly adapted baselines could do.

The claimed novelty is overstated. The method largely combines robust residual masks, segmentation priors, multi-view warping, reference selection, and pruning; the paper does not sufficiently separate what is fundamentally new from known robust reconstruction and distractor-filtering ideas.

The reported gains are promising but not decisive enough for a top-tier acceptance: results are concentrated on a few scenes, per-scene breakdowns and variance are limited, and some improvements over strong masking baselines are modest relative to the methodological complexity.

Reproducibility is weak at submission time. Code is only promised after publication, several hyperparameters and implementation choices are missing or vague, and the synthetic data construction/evaluation details are insufficient to independently validate the central claims.

Presentation quality is below the expected bar. The manuscript contains many grammatical errors, awkward wording, typos, notation problems, cramped figures/tables, and overclaiming, which together obscure the actual contribution and make the paper difficult to trust.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and practical problem: handling transient distractors in feed-forward/generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, separating both training-time instability and inference-time artifacts.

The reference-based mask prediction idea is conceptually strong: using re-rendered reference consistency to filter residual-based masks is well motivated and fits the generalizable setting better than per-scene optimization methods.

The empirical section is fairly substantial, with comparisons to retrained generalizable baselines, adapted distractor-free methods, pretrained models, synthetic data, fine-tuning experiments, efficiency analysis, and component ablations.
The paper includes useful failure-case discussion and acknowledges limitations under common occlusion and efficiency overhead.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are somewhat overstated. In particular, claims of outperforming scene-specific distractor-free methods are not fully supported by fair like-for-like evaluation, since several baselines are adapted or stripped of key per-scene components.

The evaluation is still narrow for a generalizable reconstruction claim: low-resolution inputs, limited real datasets/scenes, and mostly PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS against available clean views leave uncertainty about robustness in broader in-the-wild captures.

The method relies on several assumptions and external components, including known poses, nearby image pools, pretrained segmentation, cached masks, and sufficient view coverage; the practical failure modes under poor pose quality or sparse/dense distractors are not deeply studied.
The synthetic dataset construction appears to use 2D object insertion, which may not faithfully test 3D transient-object geometry or occlusion behavior.
